According to the law, the MUP had to hand over all the prisoners to the army, and those who were imprisoned next to the road in Konjevic Polje, they were all handed over to the army, they were boarded on buses and transported to the barracks in accordance with the request of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I misspoke, I'm sorry, 1500 prisoners taken by the MUP going to Zvornik, that's not right, probably a lot of those ended up being murdered in Kravica that same day while you were with Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At the time, I wasn't aware of that at all, that incident in Kravica. And what I saw, I saw the lawful handing over of prisoners from the MUP who had been taken prisoner next to -- along the road in Konjevic Polje. They were handed over to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go through 14 July now. You wake up, you're in the Vidikovac; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That day, you travel to Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And from there you go to Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you go all the way down to Zeleni Jadar; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And from Bratunac to Srebrenica, you go with Vasic and Borovcanin; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From Bratunac to Srebrenica, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Also to Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went straight -- actually, we passed by Srebrenica, went to Zeleni Jadar, and then we returned to Srebrenica after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I asked you in -- I didn't ask you, sorry. In your 2010 interview, you were asked what time of day did you go to Bratunac and Srebrenica from Zvornik, and you said: I think it was around 10.00 or 11.00. That's 25350, e-court 135 to 136. Is that right, about 10.00 or 11.00, you head off for Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set out at around that time because in the morning I had a meeting at Vidikovac, I remember that quite well, and at some point I set out. I think it was close to 11.00 when I set out from Vidikovac in the direction of Bratunac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And that means you make the turn at Konjevic Polje and then head to Bratunac down the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So on the 14 July, you drive right past the Kravica warehouse, sometime around noon; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around noon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you don't see anything; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Here is what Karadzic's other witnesses he's called in this trial say about what was going on when you drove past -- or what was going on at the morning of the Kravica warehouse. Jovan Nikolic, at T25493, said that he went to Kravica around 9.30 or 10.00 in the morning and witnessed an execution of ten Muslims in front of the warehouse. Did you know that, there had been an execution right before you drove by?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Aleksandar Tesic spoke about this at T35324 to 35326. He said he left Bratunac going to Zvornik, opposite of you, he also leaves between 10.00 and 12.00, he says, maybe about 11.00, and outside the Kravica warehouse, he said he didn't witness an execution. Jovan Nikolic apparently there a little bit earlier. Here is what he said he saw, same day, same approximate time that you're driving by: "When I happened upon that spot, I realised there was quite a crowd, many soldiers milling about and the bus was moving at a very slow pace, halting along the way. There is the perimeter wall of the co-op building and there were very many bodies lying there. When I think back, I realise it was a huge shock to me and particularly to those young men who were with me, aged no more than 18. I figure there must have been at least between 200 and 300 bodies lying there about a metre and a metre and a half high. At first I thought it was firewood stacked against a wall when I first cast a glance in that direction, and then I realised what it was. So it really left a horrible impression on us. "Q. Yeah. And there were a lot of soldiers there too, you said. You said there were so many that it was hard to drive through. "Yes." So how do you miss the hundreds of bodies piled up in front of the warehouse that Karadzic's other truthful witness told us about?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I don't know about the time when he passed, but at the moment when I came along, around noon, I don't think that that was there any longer. I'm telling you that from my present perspective. I think that's the reason why I didn't come across that. I think that around 12.00 that was not there any longer. I didn't pay any attention, nor did I notice it. But if it had been so marked I would have seen it. Judging by what I learned later, I think that by noon, this -- those bodies were removed from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From what you learned later, okay, that means that you would have been going past Glogova where those bodies were bulldozed into a hole at the time. How long do you think it takes to clean up hundreds and hundreds of bodies and bury them a few kilometres away? Because Glogova is closer to Bratunac. You passed that, too, on the way to Bratunac on the morning of the 14th. Did you see anybody being buried there?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't pay any attention, but I didn't register that, no. At that moment, we can talk about what I learned later on, but at that time, around 12.00, as I was passing along, I never noticed that. I mean, it was really crowded that whole area, movements of tanks and the army, withdrawing from Srebrenica, moving along the road, but I -- there was a big crowd but I didn't notice this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Same day, 14 July, let me read out to you -- well, let me -- let me -- let me do it this way, I want to ask you a question. This is something I read to you in the interview, okay? I read you when we met what Vasic had testified to in the Perisic case, which was that on the 14th, at 7.00 in the morning, he arrived at the Bratunac station because he'd received information that minister of internal affairs, Mr. Tomislav Kovac, was going to visit Bratunac and Srebrenica that day. I had the intention to prepare for this visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, this is 25303 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because of the time I'm going to have to move very quickly. He is asked: "What did Colonel Beara tell you? "A. He repeated that on the next -- that the order of General Mladic to him was to kill the prisoners. And he asked if I could set aside a few trusty or trusted policemen who would be placed under his command in order to carry out this task. I said that I was not going to give any police officers policemen for that. As far as I understood the order was not such and that I did not wish to participate in something like that. He turned away angrily and left." And then he says -- he's asked: "Later on when you met Minister Kovac, did you relate your conversation with Beara, and we know that Minister Kovac came to Bratunac that morning; is that right?" And Vasic answers under oath in Perisic: "Immediately after the minister's arrival, Minister Kovac's arrival, I informed him about my meeting and the content of the conversation and the content, actually, of what I heard from Beara. "Q. Did he react at all? "A. The minister said that the military prisoners were under the jurisdiction of the army and that was not our job and that he shouldn't interfere with these matters." And then he's asked later -- I won't read it out again, but I read it to you in the interview that whether he repeated all of the details and all of that verbatim to you, and he said he did. In your 2010 interview, this is 65 ter 25350, e-court page 34, I asked you this question: "Q. Okay. Just to be absolutely clear, we talked about your conversation with Vasic and whether he spoke to you in person or a message. Did he or did he not tell you expressly that Beara had requested men for the MUP to be used for executions and that you had explicitly said no?" Your answer was: "I -- I don't think -- I cannot be sure whether Vasic told me this or was it Mane Djuric who told me this first. I cannot really remember now who was the first." We only have English: "Q. One second. But to be clear, you did know that Beara was looking for or was requesting MUP people for executions, is it correct? "A. At one moment, I did learn that Beara was looking for men from the MUP and that he would abuse -- in killing of these prisoners and I think Mane told me this." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, you talk about a sequence of events. You said that I mentioned Mane -- Vasic and Mane and the meeting with Beara, so all of this what you listed now does not really correspond with the actual situation, and what was going on. In Bratunac, when I -- we can't -- this is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bratunac, Vasic did not report to me about this possibility in this way. On arrival to Bratunac, it was requested for me to meet the Crisis Staff and Deronjic. I didn't want to meet any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but maybe we are entering into a very delicate situation right here. And of course I cannot predict what question would follow this, and of course I might try to predict what Mr. Kovac's answer would be to this, but I cannot be sure about that. Maybe it would be wise just to go to private session because maybe I will be in a position to advise Mr. Kovac to use his right to -- for privilege against not to incriminate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I followed Mr. Lazarevic's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I gave him the advice about his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: ] Maybe I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour clearly advised Mr. Kovac about his right when testified before this Tribunal, and of course about his right not to incriminate himself with certain answers. If need be, with this line of question, we might be in a position that Mr. Kovac, through some answer, might have said something which could be used against him. This is why I was intervening right this moment in order to make sure that in such a situation, Your Honour closed the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in paragraph 124 of his statement, which he adopted today after being warned and swore to and said his answers would be the same - so it is, in fact, his testimony - he says: I was informed that prisoners from Srebrenica had been taken to Zvornik. One day, perhaps 14 July, Mane Djuric told me that Colonel Beara had requested a police unit - I'm sorry, I'm going too fast - and that Chief Vasic and Djuric worried that the unit might be used for illegal activities including liquidation of prisoners. When I heard this, I ordered the police to cease communications with the military security organ and not to be invoked in any way in their -- involved - Freudian slip - in any way in their activities. So he was warned. He left this in his statement and swore to it. He has waived on this entire issue of what Vasic and Djuric told him about Beara. He can't go halfway into the conversation. And this is a well established principle. I don't want to argue all the law now. But when you talk about fact X, and fact Y is directly linked to it, if you didn't raise a privilege as to fact X, you've waved to fact Y.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think now the witness, Mr. Kovac, has understood the situation. It is for him to provoke his privilege against self-incrimination, and he -- when he -- when he invokes that privilege we will consider the matter later on. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe if I ask the question again, put us back where we were quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, the Chamber is minded to extend your time so do not be pushed by time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think there is a separate issue here and which is what was being raised by Mr. Lazarevic, and that is whether evidence should be heard in private session because this Chamber can make an order under Rule 90(E) about protection of a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When the witness refuses to answer the question on the ground of danger of self-incrimination, we will consider that issue when requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So far, the witness has testified voluntarily on the advice given by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. But if the witness is willing to answer a question but believes that it would be necessary to protect his rights by having an answer in private session, he should be able to do that also. It's not necessary to invoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's all premature. We haven't heard anything from the witness. And I think -- yes. Shall we stop here and continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I read out an interview where you said about Beara requesting men for the MUP to be used for executions that you said, I can't be sure whether Vasic told me this, or was it Mane Djuric who told me this first. I can't remember now who was the first. And your other answer that, At one moment I did learn that Beara was looking for men from the MUP, and he would abuse in killing of these prisoners, and I think Mane told me this. And my question is: Do you stand by that, that's true, that Mane or Vasic told you that Beara was looking for MUP to help execute prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, you have asked me ten questions in the meantime, and given answers to them too. My stay in Bratunac, Vasic's briefing to me in Bratunac, about his meeting with Vasic, I don't know what I have to state my mind about, because you've brought me to five different points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him continue. I'll give you ample time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, the whole problem in the testimony, it's not the problem of truth. The problem is the attitude of the OTP to me, for ten years now. Because it's not in their interest that I as someone who can give a valid testimony about the situation -- they simply didn't give me an opportunity and didn't allow me to because they kept side tracking me. The substance is this: During my stay in Bratunac, I did not want to meet with, nor did I meet Deronjic or Beara or anyone from those Crisis Staffs. I didn't even want to enter the police station in Bratunac, because that was my official attitude. I did not want to meddle with their activities and I made Vasic clearly aware of that. I only picked up Borovcanin and Vasic and we went to Srebrenica to establish the police station there, and I visited the main facilities, and that was all the information I had on that day. As for the report on the meeting between Vasic and Beara about what Vasic reported to anyone, these meetings, I didn't allow him to because his stay work with them in the area covered by the centre is one thing, but linking up with Beara in any way, especially in view of my relations with that man and his service, and let me tell you also that during the war I never met Beara, he was the chief of the military security and I was the chief of the public security throughout the war, the two of us never met, and there are reasons why we didn't. And if you ask me whether at any moment I had, and if you want to connect this you will have a clear story, if at any moment, but not on that day, but perhaps two days later I was informed by the deputy chief of the centre, among other things, Mane, that Beara had been looking for a certain number of men, requesting them from the centre of MUP and that there was a possibility that he could abuse these men. My answer at the time was fully, as I have already said, clearly, negative. You must not co-operate at any cost because it's unlawful. You must not co-operate with Beara and resubordinate men to him because it's not in accordance with the law. The law defines clearly how men can be resubordinated. At the moment, seeing that, and knowing Beara, and knowing from experience with that man what sort of a character he was, independently from any assessment about what could happen or not, I told them then because it's -- one could not exclude the possibility that this man could abuse men, not only prisoners of war but anyone, because he was that sort of personality, I prohibited them expressly to communicate with him in any way whatsoever and have any sort of agreements with them. And I prohibited them from co-operating with him and his service. I prohibited them to co-operate with him. That was explicit on that day, but it wasn't on that day when I visited but a day or two later when they called me. There is an intercept between Beara and Krstic where they state clearly that someone is not allowing them to do something. The person who didn't allow them to do something because of the possibility that they may abuse it was myself. And even though there was no need for me to close it off, up until that time, but it's a matter of what happened first, what happened later, and the point of view of the OTP for ten years now because you feel this need to connect it all into some sort of joint criminal enterprise, and something that you could not believe up until this day, but there is the Chamber as well, it's in my interest too, up until this moment and now as well to say it clearly. This is precisely this relation that I and the military security service had, between myself and the Supreme Command, or rather, the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. A joint criminal enterprise could never have happened. We could have made mistakes but this was not possible. And it's true that I gave such orders. And if this act that I ordered them that the police should not be used for such things at any cost, at the very thought that they could be used if that would be incriminating for me, I am willing to accept that, in the way as I have told you about it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement with you, Mr. Kovac? Paragraph 124. Here in your statement, which you confirmed, you said: "One day, perhaps on 14th July, Mane Djuric told me that Beara had requested a police unit." And now you're saying it was one or two days later. Are you changing your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not changing it. It's just that my stay on the 14th there is one thing. I'm not changing it. I'm just telling you that on the 14th, Mane Djuric was at the seat of the centre. He was not in Bratunac. When I stayed in Bratunac and Srebrenica I did not have this piece of information. I learned that later on in a telephone conversation with Mane Djuric so that was afterwards. Whether that was in the night between the 14th and the 15th, around that period, we could find it by analysing the intercept between Beara and Krstic, when exactly that took place. You have that and it can be checked and then it can be specified. It could have been in the night between the 14th and the 15th. That was the time frame. But I don't think it was -- it wasn't on the 14th at noon. Mane Djuric was at the centre seat. He wasn't in Bratunac or in Srebrenica. He was in the seat of the centre in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You meet Vasic in Bratunac when you arrive there on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He has learned from Beara, according to himself and other evidence, that Beara intends to kill the prisoners held in Bratunac. Do you expect the chief of the Zvornik CJB, upon learning of a plan by the army to commit mass murder and requesting MUP units to help, would inform the deputy minister when he meets him that same day?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have -- he never reported to me that he had information that Beara intended to execute prisoners of war in an organised manner. Even on that day Vasic did not talk to me about that. On that day, he didn't talk to me about this in Bratunac. Regardless of whether Vasic stated something different from that about that day and conversation with me, but he did not report to me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. While you're in Bratunac on the 14th, you meet Borovcanin in a restaurant; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I did not want to enter the police station or the municipality on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he tells you that prisoners were liquidated, murdered, in Kravica the day before; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reported to me that one of his specials had been killed and that the unit commander had been wounded. He also reported to me that an incident occurred in which the prisoners had attacked the policemen who were securing them and that in this incident it happened that one policeman was wounded and one was killed and that a number of -- though he did not specify the number, he just said that those who had launched the attack, that the special policemen liquidated them. Several -- several men in principle, he said there were several people, and that was what he reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So you knew the Special Police had murdered prisoners when you were in Bratunac on the 14th. Forget the number. You knew that there had been a terrible war crime committed by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. At that time, I was aware of the incident that happened; namely, that prisoners had attacked MUP members who were guarding them. That's what I was told, that an incident had occurred. One policeman was killed, one policeman was wounded, the guards had been attacked, that's the information I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, when I asked you about the Kravica warehouse executions in 2010, not I -- but you were asked - 65 ter 25350 - in connection with the Petrovic Pirocanac video taken, you said -- this is e-court pages 143 to 144. And let me say one more thing, I was neither furious nor was I mad that this footage had been taken. I did not like the fact that people were killed and I was mad that this happened to a MUP unit, although it was under the command of the army, and we could never wash ourselves from this. This is my attitude, and I think it's correct. So you agree that the MUP can never wash itself from the killings at Kravica, even though it was resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to go back to the 14th, when I read out to you how Vasic had explained and testified how he immediately informed you of the plan to -- Beara's plan to kill prisoners, when you arrived on the 14th, and you said you weren't sure whether it was Vasic or Mane, why don't you tell me it was the night of the 14th or the 15th? And why isn't that in your statement for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything important in the sequence of events, but it's sure that Vasic did not inform me that day in Bratunac. And I'm sure, as I'm testifying here, that I spoke to Mane Djuric on the phone about the fact that Beara had requested a certain number of people who were to be engaged, and their suspicions that these men could be put to wrongful use. That was a telephone conversation with Mane Djuric. He got my answer, and after that you have the intercept between Beara and Krstic where they clearly say that the chief of police is not giving them these men. And that is the situation that is very easy to understand. It's very easy to connect the dots. You have all the evidence led in this trial and other trials. I am here to clear that situation up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That night, at 22.45 to 23.10, after your trip to the field ordered by Karadzic, you meet with him in his office - that's P02242, page 91, right? - the night of the 14th, 10.45 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let's get one thing clear. I didn't go into any field missions on Karadzic's order at that time. It was not part of my work style to do that. I was not occupying the position of a commissioner or something, to go into the field. I had to set up a police station, but I could have sent somebody else to do that. The order didn't state anywhere that I had to go personally, but I decided myself to go to Srebrenica to set up that police station. It was my decision. It was not that Karadzic sent me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were with him at 22.45 to 23.10. That was the question, right? You were with him that night?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably. I believe that I was there almost every day between those hours. Yes, yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because your previous statement -- I'm going to read you back again your testimony in the Jevic case; 25516, is the 65 ter number, English 24 to 25, B/C/S 25 to 26: "So I went into the field acting on orders of the president of the republic and with the intention of finding out about the situation in the town and about the state of industrial facilities."

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I see it, the president issued this order. In fact, it can't be an order. It's a legal provision that a police station should be set up. That was the instruction I received from the president, and that was back on the 12th, so I issued instructions myself to set up and organise a police station, and I myself went out to set up that police station. So there is no doubt that on the 14th I was in the area of Srebrenica and Zeleni Jadar. I was there officially because that was part of my responsibility. I didn't go to Bratunac, and I didn't have any official talks there. That was not my job. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And -- well, I don't know that, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The second day in a row, day two of the murder operation, 14 July, the day after your meeting with General Mladic, same day you met with Vasic and Borovcanin, when you know and Karadzic knows that the MUP has been taking a huge amount of prisoners, when you know and he knows that they have been sent to Zvornik, you meet with him after coming back from Srebrenica and talk about ammunition problems in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the ammunition problem in Sarajevo. There was also a broader problem. It was not just ammunition. It was a problem with the entire theatre of war. It's very hard to explain now in response to your question how Srebrenica was connected with Sarajevo. Tactically, the attack of Muslims on Sarajevo and Srebrenica were connected, and my responsibility was Sarajevo; whereas the other people who were there clearly had some responsibility for Srebrenica and others simply assumed that responsibility of their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many other days in the war can you tell me or point to reports of the Special Police taking, you know, over a thousand prisoners, with the number increasing?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have the reports of the special unit? Because I don't have them, except that one which you showed which they drafted by chance. And even concerning that report, I was not able to recollect it. A special brigade did not send reports throughout. You have that one. Do you have any others? Because I don't know. If you have them, help me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How about answering the question? How many other days of war can you tell me or point me to -- let's just say you're learning Special Police are taking numbers of prisoners, of a thousand, with the number increasing.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with this statement that the Special Police unit took prisoners. They didn't take any prisoners. It was a joint operation, a military operation, in which they participated. I cannot accept that the special unit took prisoners. So I cannot point out to any other -- any other days in the war. Do you mean Srebrenica? Do you mean other theatres of war? What am I supposed to compare it to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You as deputy minister who was in the field, who was with Borovcanin, who received that report, as you sit here today in 2013, you can't agree that the Special Police took prisoners on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit and the people who were resubordinated to the army took prisoners, as did others who were resubordinated. They took prisoners and turned them over to the security organ. What happened later, we all know. Nobody is disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nobody is disputing, let's go to that. Nobody is disputing. We all know that the VRS carried out mass executions of prisoners following the fall of Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, 14 July, night of the 14th into the 15th, you spent the night -- this isn't in your statement. You don't go into 14th and 15th night -- morning of the 15th. You're back at the Vidikovac; right? You said that in your interviews. You got the rash in Srebrenica? Do you want me to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the rash is important, yes, it's probably so. I was making way through Zeleni Jadar and many destroyed farms and the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The rash isn't important. It's just to help you remember. Because you said in your 2003 interview, ten years ago -- this is 65 ter 22146, at English pages 120 to 121, and B/C/S page 136. In this context: "Okay, what happened next on the 14 July?" Answer from you: "I went back to Vidikovac motel, and I remember clearly that my hands were somehow covered with some kind of rash or something, because I was taking some documents from the police station to Srebrenica and they were so dirty, and I guess I had some kind of infection or something so I had a shower." And then later on in that same interview you talk about being there and on the 15th. S on the -- does that help you remember that on the 14th you spent the night at the Vidikovac again?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I was there briefly. At that time, I was moving intensively around the area every day, Vidikovac, Pale, perhaps I spent a few hours there. I probably was there, but I think I spent the night between the 13th and the 14th at the Vidikovac. That's the night I spent there. As for the other days, how much time I spent there, I don't know if I stated when my memory was more fresh that I was there at that time, it's probably true. I don't know what you want to ask. Is there a particular situation you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You answered that you think you were probably there, because on the 14th of July, in Zvornik, in Vidikovac, where you are again after coming back from Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica, that's the big execution day at Orahovac, where over a thousand prisoners who were bought to the Vidikovac hotel that you stay at, are sent from there to the school in Orahovac and executed.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. When I stayed at the Vidikovac motel -- no, that's not true. At the Vidikovac motel, there was nobody except for a couple of employees. So technically, it was not possible. It was a very small area that somebody came to Vidikovac when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me tell you what our case is. You've already confirmed that you spent the night of the 13th to 14th in the Vidikovac, right, 13th, to 14th; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On the 14th in the morning, Vasic is in Bratunac when the huge convoy of prisoners from Bratunac is brought to Zvornik, Mane Djuric has testified -- I didn't expect to do this so I don't have the cite. He's testified that he was at the Vidikovac hotel when this group of prisoners arrived. So my point is you've got MUP at one end, MUP at the other end, and you are at Vidikovac on the 14th in the morning, and at some other point on the day that the prisoners arrive. Are you telling me you didn't know the prisoners arrived at the Vidikovac hotel on the 14th of July, 1995, from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible that they came to Vidikovac hotel. Vidikovac hotel has a surface of just a couple of hundred square metres and several rooms. They could have passed by the hotel on their way to the barracks in Zvornik. I believe that is completely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me be clear. They didn't come and check in. They didn't stay the night. They were on buses and trucks parked there because there is a big, broad parking lot in front of the Vidikovac hotel and they stayed along the road. My point is that was the end point for the convoy, not that they got off the buses and trucks and went into the hotel. Do you not know that, that the convoy went to the Vidikovac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. And it couldn't have been their end point. The end point could have been only the barracks of Zvornik. There is a thoroughfare outside the Vidikovac hotel. What you're putting to me has absolutely nothing to do with reality. You keep trying to connect these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me be clear. I don't mean it's the end point or the end of their journey. The end of their journey are the various execution sites they are murdered at. What I mean is they come from Bratunac to Zvornik, that's where the convoy stops at the Vidikovac hotel, and from there, they are shipped out in buses and trucks to Orahovac, Kozluk, Pilica, places like that. You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. At that place, Vidikovac hotel, that from that place they were shipped out -- no, no, they were at the barracks, and at that parking lot, that was not doable. Vidikovac motel is at the entry to the town of Zvornik. Whether somebody stopped these buses before they were allowed to go into town, what the army did, I don't know. But this connection that you are trying to make with the shipping out of people from these buses and the very few men from MUP who were there, that connection is not possible. That is not true. People from MUP were at Vidikovac, not people from the army. And those MUP men were dealing with completely different things. You cannot connect this facility with any of that business. It's pure insinuation, innuendo on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you something that's not pure insinuation or innuendo on my part, which is the evidence in this case, that when the prisoners on buses arrived at the school in Orahovac, where they stayed briefly before being murdered 700 metres away, there were escorts on those buses that were civilian MUP police, some of whom were from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know that policemen were the escorts. I have no reports to that effect. That they were brought to be executed and escorted by policemen, I don't know that. That could not have happened, that policemen should have done that, that they had participated in this. That's impossible. That they guarded the buses up to the town of Zvornik or whatever point they were turned over to the army where the triage of prisoners was effected, that's quite possible. It was quite normal for police escorts to be provided during transport but that policemen were involved in taking prisoners to execution sites, that could not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just make a cite to what I was referring to. That's P00379. T6446, 6449, 6475 to 6476 of the transcript pages of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well: "That they guarded the buses up to the town of Zvornik or whatever point they were turned over to the army where the triage of prisoners was effected, that's quite possible. It was quite normal ..." Is it quite possible and quite normal that the police escort, the buses to Zvornik, when the chief of the Zvornik centre, Vasic, is in Bratunac, and he's just spoken with Beara and he's just spoken with Deronjic and he knows that they are all being sent to Zvornik to be murdered, is it still okay to escort them?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Vasic knew at that time that they were all going to be murdered. I don't believe that's true. And I don't think the police would have ever guarded any convoy in which some people were intended for killing. We are talking about Zvornik here. They had clear instructions from the army, and the army was organising and doing everything, that the prisoners -- in fact the buses who were coming to pick them up, would go exclusively to the barracks in Zvornik. I explicitly asked them about that. And it's quite normal for prisoners to be directed to a military installation, the barracks in Zvornik. And that is the information that was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, very quickly before the break, 15 July, 16.15 to sometime 17.40 something, this is P02242, page 92, you meet with Karadzic again. That's in his diary and we've already discussed that you met him on those days. Now, by your own testimony just a little while ago, today, you said, moving it later, that it was, you think, the night between 14th and the 15th that you heard from Mane Djuric about Beara's requesting MUP to participate in executions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What objection is it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Esteemed Mr. Nicholls is really making great efforts, and I appreciate them because he's doing even more than necessary, but it was really not said that Mane Djuric had been informed that these men would be participating in executions. It was just said that Beara requested them, and execution is not the only possible misuse in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that's a proper intervention. I don't know what the intervention was. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've already said that the 15 July -- never mind. You meet with Karadzic on the 14th or 15th. You've been informed, according to your own statement to the Defence and to what you testified here to today, about this request from Beara to use MUP for executions or -- and you don't raise that with the president, with the Supreme Commander. You don't say as the highest law enforcement official in the country, I think I ought to tell you that the army is planning to liquidate prisoners.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the plan, and I don't believe the plan existed for the army to liquidate prisoners. That information that one small unit of the police could be put to wrongful use did not give me a basis to suggest or suppose that they could be involved in mass executions. When I ordered the security centre and all the command structures not to co-operate with Beara, I considered the problem solved. What I expected from him is low-level misuse, and I thought that he was prepared to misuse the police, not only against the Muslims and -- but also against Serbs and others, because that's the kind of man he was. That's the kind of man I knew him to be. I had no reason to believe that they were planning mass executions and killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So you protested in the beginning to the MUP being engaged at all, according to you, when you meet with Karadzic on 9 July and the MUP are engaged, and then you get a report from the deputy in Zvornik that he thinks Beara, taking it most charitably in your statement, was worried that the unit might be used for illegal activities including liquidations of prisoners. That's what it says in paragraph 124 of your statement. You don't think it's important for you as the highest acting law enforcement officer to tell the president that you've just heard the Main Staff wants -- may use the MUP to execute prisoners and that you ordered them not to take part?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I would appreciate it very much if you would refrain from making these constructions, if you want an answer from me. I did not understand it as a request from the Main Staff. It was conveyed to me that way, and that's the way I understood it. I saw Beara as a petty manipulator in view of what he had done before, a man bent on crime, who was involved in crimes against the Serbs in the past. I had no idea that he was capable of such great evil. Whereas you have a different perspective. You are looking at it with 18 years' hindsight. You know how things happened. I, at the time, was involved in operations around Sarajevo and I had only as much information as reached me at the time. I was unable physically and legally to deal with army things, and I must say also in their defence that up to that time, our army had never acted in contravention of all the international conventions and the law. I had no reason to believe that they would begin then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break? Will we need the next witness for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be nice if we could reach him but can we find out how much longer you're going to allow the Prosecution to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It also may depend on how much time Mr. Karadzic is going to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if we can have some indication from how much the Prosecution will use, we can calculate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's very hard to say, but I think approximately 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will release the next witness. We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just briefly at page 64, line 21 today, I referred to a part of Mane Djuric's testimony and said I didn't have the cite at the time because I wasn't expecting to use it. That was 7 March 2013, at T35041 to 35043, that I was thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to now ask you again, talking about your meetings with President Karadzic on 14, 15, July, okay? That's what I'm talking about. Understand? That's what my next question will be about.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we asked you, you were asked in 2010 in your interview, 65 ter 25350, at e-court page 43, in the context of why you did not discuss murders and Beara's request with Karadzic during your meetings, and you were asked this question: "So let me get this straight. Is the reason you are saying that you did not discuss or protest to the president what was happening with the army killing people was because you thought he already knew from all these other sources?" And your answer was: "This is crystal clear, because he had Bajagic, who knew everything. He had Deronjic. He received all the information that he needed from them. He had the entire nomenclature there, people who knew everything and controlled everything." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely stand by that statement, that they could have informed him about Srebrenica itself, because Deronjic and other structures of military security, in particular, were directly involved in the processes that were evolving in the area. I meant in official terms; that is to say the Main Staff, the service, Deronjic. They were duty-bound to inform him about everything that was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, this is about your testimony under oath in the Mitrovic case, 65 ter 25515, e-court page 43 of the English, B/C/S 52. This is speaking about your trip to Bratunac on the 14th: "Defence counsel Jaksic: You said that you did not meet with the civilian leadership. Did you meet with Mr. Deronjic who had been appointed civilian commissioner for Srebrenica municipality? Perhaps I might make a slight mistake in the name of this appointment. Did you have an opportunity to meet Mr. Deronjic? "Witness Kovac: I did not meet with him, nor did I wish to meet with him. Defence counsel Jaksic: Why didn't you wish to meet with him?" Witness Kovac, your answer: "Well I had fought for years against these para-Crisis Staffs, these para-commissioners, and para-authorities, para-police forces, and I simply saw that these days he greatly intensified his contacts with the president, intensively providing him information, from security information to all other kinds. And I always knew what that was leading to." And I'll stop reading there. Do you stand by that testimony you gave?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely stand by that being my attitude, but I was not officially in charge of meeting with him. I did not have an official task to meet with him or an official duty. But my attitude towards local structures, towards people, that is to say these ad hoc functions, well, I don't know whether it's right or not, but that was the attitude I had throughout the war, and that's why I could never be appointed minister formally through the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you also agree with the part where you say about

utterances.speaker: MR. DERONJIC
utterances.text: And I simply saw in these days he greatly intensified his contacts with the president, intensively providing him with information. Were you telling the truth when you testified there to that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that he came. Now, what kind of talks he had with the president, I don't know. I don't know -- I don't know about the content of his talks with the president. But I did see him come because in certain time intervals, he appeared in the president's office, when I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. My point is you stand by that prior testimony you gave under oath - yes or no? - with the explanations you've given?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by him having come to the president, but I don't know about the content of the information that he gave. I can assume that he informed him about the situation, he certainly informed him about the situation in Srebrenica, but I am not aware of the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. In September 1995, you allegedly carry out your own investigation into Srebrenica events as requested by Jovica Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, did you have an opportunity of hearing Jovica on that? I would not say allegedly. I did not carry out an investigation on the basis of the law because I was not in a position to do so, but I did collect information about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you found out then and confirmed that Mladic and Beara had had prisoners killed. You knew that in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, at that time, I had unverified information; That is to say from certain people in certain structures, that first of all Beara, Beara, Beara was the operative, and I think that the main ideologue too, of the execution of the prisoners and this entire situation that happened in the Srebrenica action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. This is your 2010 interview, 65 ter 25350, e-court pages 75 to 76, you were asked about this September 1995 investigation. And you answer a question saying you were asked to investigate whether any Serb forces took part in the fall of Srebrenica. That's not what my question was about, whether any Serb forces took part. You were asked: "Okay, when was this conveyed to you?" Your answer: "Somewhere in September 1995." Question: "And that's when everybody knew that thousands of prisoners had been executed?" And your answer was: "Probably, probably everyone knew. I did." You were telling the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I knew, and my statement probably could be that I do not have any confirmation as to who knew and to what extent. Let me be precise, at the end of September and October up until mid-November, all the time I carried out operative investigations as to the causes, where the orders had come from for the overall operation, whether there were any forces from Serbia present there. So these were the basic global elements that Mr. Stanisic was interested in because he said to me that he was preparing for the Dayton conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're going well beyond the answer. Thank you. And you were also asked this in the same interview at page 81. During this investigation, you sent people to do this investigation. Did you send them also to the field to check possible execution sites? Here was your answer: "No, there was no need for that. I asked my operatives to conduct investigation. There was no need for them to go to the possible execution sites because I needed answers to the questions who issued an order to kill these people and how this did -- how did this order come about, and also how did the order to attack Srebrenica come about." Question: "Okay." Answer: "This is the part I'm interested in. This is the only question. Of course, the locations, the site of the executions were known at the time. And that is why there was no need to conduct an investigation to this extent." Do you stand by that answer where you said you didn't send anybody to check execution sites because they were already known?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no, because already in the stage of operative gathering of information, it was secret. To identify the execution sites specifically would open entirely new dimensions and would go beyond my powers, and in that stage I was not dealing with that. You know, that was the first stage. You know that in every stage, first of all, you collect operative information, and only then you carry out further preparations for official reporting and official proposals as to which organs are supposed to be involved. And then this operative activity of mine stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. This is what you said, talking about September 1995. Of course, the locations, the sites of the executions were known at the time. And that is why there was no need to conduct an investigation to this extent. You said yesterday you clearly told the truth in your interviews. Were you telling the truth or lying when you said here that the execution sites were known at the time, September 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just tell the truth, but you put questions that no matter what I say by way of a response, it turns out that I'm not telling the truth. Now, this is one thing. If I collected information for me, then this information was collected for me. And at that moment, in that initial stage, because I myself personally dealt with this collecting of information, so partly this was known and other things that I was supposed to gather, well, we were supposed to conduct interviews with important protagonists and secretly at that because this would have been a threat to their lives and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. Again, of course, the locations, the sites of the executions, were known at the time and that -- and that is why there was no need to conduct an investigation to this extent. That was an answer to a question whether you sent anybody to look at the execution sites. Your answer was: "Of course the locations, the sites of the executions, were known at the time." So my question is: Were you telling the truth at that time in September 1995, you knew where the execution sites were?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, you are changing theses now. What -- there is this one operative gathering information for me and this secret operative gathering information. Now you're changing positions as if there were some public investigation going on, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure you understood. This is what you told to the investigator during your interview. I'll read it to you. Just hear. This is your answer: "Of course the locations, the sites of the executions, were known at the time." Do you confirm having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way -- I mean what I meant. So if there is secret operative gathering of information, that was done for me and a third person, that is secret. And now this is as if something was known publicly so it wasn't operatives that went in the direction of checking that, because this part of the information is something I already had; that is to say, I had this through direct contacts so this operation of operative gathering was carried out by me and a few other operatives. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it was a secret operative or not, you knew the locations of execution sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I worked on the direct gathering of information, at the time I received information from certain persons concerning a few of these important sites, so I had this information within this gathering of information. That's why the operatives did not go into that direction. It's not that something was publicly known about these locations:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop talking about the public. I'm asking if you knew as you stated here -- and you stated before that you told the truth in the interviews. Did you know about the locations of the execution sites, you, Tomo Kovac, in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of September, I personally received information and I then knew what the execution sites were. And that is why I did not send operatives and I did not expose these people to security risks, to work on that. I think that this matter is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? Known. That means in public. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's clear. So the question was whether the witness knew and he confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were minister at that point, not deputy minister, right, in September 1995. You'd been promoted.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The same interview, page 64, you were asked why you did not tell Karadzic about this investigation you were carrying out. And you said: I cannot explain why I didn't tell him. And then you go on. And what I want to know is why, as minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, in September 1995, you did not, according to you, discuss the locations of the execution sites with the Supreme Commander, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask to have the original in Serbian shown to the witness? There is no reason for him to look at the English version. I need the original too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the interview is transcribed only in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably there may exist the audio tape if they want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In any event, forget the transcript. Forget what I read out to you. Let's keep it really simple. You've already said why in September 1995, as the highest law enforcement official in the Republika Srpska, did you not discuss, tell, the President of Republika Srpska about the locations of execution sites?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me -- if you allow me to say -- this operative investigation started at the end of 1995, or, rather, the end of September 1995. I did not complete it. My activity on that stopped on 21 November 1995, after the accident I had with the military vehicle in Vlasenica, when I had a concussion and when my escort was killed. If you know everything, you must have that report from the hospital too. My operative investigation stopped then and soon after that I was replaced. So I'm looking at September and October. And we are talking about this secret investigation. We are not talking about any kind of official investigation. We are talking about a delicate investigation, and all the people who took part in this had their lives in danger at the time. So, please, do not put things that way to me, that I'm doing that. It is certain that had I stayed on there and further on in some other stages after that, this would have reached the president of the republic too, but I already told you how I conducted and ended my work at the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's just make it clear. This is the kind of policeman you are, this is the kind of career policeman you are, this is the kind of minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, that you know about execution sites and you don't even, according to you, tell the president of your own state.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was collecting information. The execution sites were the end of the story, but what really mattered was the beginning, that is to say investigating what happened. There were war operations going on beforehand, but until I entered these operative investigations, I did not know the essence, the essence of what was going on in Srebrenica itself. That was the reason for my operative investigation. And if you are getting at that, if you are talking about my professional career, let me tell you that it is professional for some things to be investigated secretly and that you should not put people in such a position that they would lose their lives on account of that. I did that for a month and you've been working at this for almost 20 years and we are moving point by point to see what it is that really happened. On the other hand, this was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you've answered. Here is something you said -- well, never mind, never mind. Could I have P00164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it appeared in this transcript of interview briefly but I think it's important to put on record in this hearing as well why the witness didn't tell Mr. Karadzic at the time as to the initiation of his secret investigation. Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would not be a serious -- well, first of all, I did not think -- actually, at first, when collecting certain information, especially in this kind of situation, I did not think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put you a question more directly. You said that that -- secret operative investigation was triggered upon the request of Stanisic, who is the secret chief of Republic of Serbia, different country. If I were in your position, I would immediately inform your president that such request was forwarded, requested, by Stanisic, before you start the secret investigation. Why did you not tell Mr. Karadzic at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stanisic asked first and foremost to have the following clarified: Whether there were any forces of Serbia that had taken part in this, whether there were any police or military force that is had taken part in this action. That was the main thing that he was after. That was the main thing that he was after. On the other hand, he also wanted to know who had issued the order. Of course, as I worked on this, I extended it to the overall activity involved. Stanisic had a special role. He needed this for -- for the peace, for Dayton, because he was in charge of preparing the Dayton agreement. If you can recall, the Dayton agreement, during the preparations for the Dayton agreement, Serbia was officially involved - and how? - and its organs, including Stanisic, who was officially in charge of the preparation itself. That is one reason. The second reason is that I, in some other stage, I would have certainly informed Karadzic not as a secret report. It would be -- it would have been an official report. However, I did not have the time to do that because I was dismissed in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So was it a kind of treason on your part against Mr. Karadzic, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think it was treason. Quite simply I thought that this was the first stage in the methodology of our work. I never betrayed him throughout the war so I wouldn't have betrayed him then either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small omission in the transcript leads to a misunderstanding. The witness said I did not have the time to finish that. That is to say he didn't have time to finish the investigation, and he was dismissed in the meantime, and that's why he didn't report. However, in the transcript that is missing in line 16. He didn't have the time to finish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, do you confirm having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can also be listened to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. This is President Karadzic's April 1996 order to conduct -- April 1996 order to conduct an investigation to be carried out at the locations where the victims -- where victims of the armed conflict in and around Srebrenica are to be found. Now, you were asked if you ever started -- in your 2003 interview, you were asked -- I would like to ask you -- this is at e-court pages 133 to 134, B/C/S 151 to 153. 133 should be at the moment, 151. We don't necessarily need to bring it up. I would like ask you if you remember that such an order has been sent by the president on the 1st of April, 1996, the president of the republic, answer: That later what was done was laundering or justifying. Why had not such an order been sent in July or August of 1995? Then you were shown this document. Investigator says: I'll show you ERN 00442407. That's the document that's in front of you. Do you have any comments about this order? And you said: I do. What I can say is, as you see I don't have many documents with me, I never tried to put aside some documents. And you go on. And then you say: But so all of these post event documents that were created were just some kind of a cover-up document or, again, laundering documents. If I had been president of the republic I would have known what to do it, and all of these things that happened afterwards are just a big shame and damage to my own people. And it's just a shame, a damage to everything that we were fighting for. And if there is any responsibility that needs to be, there needs to be the individual one. Instead of this order that he issued, he should have issued an order to arrest Mladic, to lock him up. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when the president of the republic is forced -- what did I mean by laundering? When the president of the republic is forced only in April to issue an order, and before that, the government organs, the military organs, and other government organs did not officially start, though they were obliged by law to begin prosecution and establishing this. This is what I experienced in 1992, also, that they were doing the same things to the president, and there were some other things that I issued. If I had been a minister he wouldn't have had any need for such an order. But that would have been done officially, officially prosecuted and done. And the president substantially was the last instance who issued an order to them to do some things. In fact, he was trying to launder these organs and encourage them to do their work which they had failed to do. That was my view, both in 1992, and then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's why you called it a cover-up document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, not covering up. I think that it was wrong. You cannot cover up something for which you issue a public order. But what's the point here and about my position towards the judiciary organs? They are responsible because they had enough time. April was too late. They should have reacted earlier. The military security, the military judiciary, the military prosecutor's office and civilian organs also, whoever could collect any information, they should have also taken some official legal action, from bottom up towards the president, rather than the other way around, from the president towards them. So this is how I view this as a professional. Now, I don't know whether what you -- this is already 1996. I wasn't there then, but I did state my judgement about everything and I also said what I would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number for the 2003 interview, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 22146. Again page 133 of the English, and, if I'm right, it starts on 151 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that's what you mean by instead of this order that he issued, which you earlier called a cover-up, he should have issued the order to arrest Mladic to lock him up, by that you meant to convey to the investigator -- this is just like 1992. The organs below the president aren't doing their work. That's what that sentence was meant to convey? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. All the organs which are listed here as addressees from the president who were obliged by law to do all this and who are ordered now by him to do that, they should have done their work before that and they should have sent reports to the president upon completion of their work. Here we have the opposite situation, and the fall of the government or the state, because, once again, this returns him back to 1992, with this sort of attitude, because this order was not issued just like that but precisely because these organs did not function. And through this order, in fact, he turned out that he was covering up their failure to work. I would have acted differently. I would have asked for a different kind of responsibility. But, certainly, the president is a politician and I'm looking at this as a lawyer and as a policeman, how I would have dealt with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We agree, as you sit -- well, strike that. Are you aware of any investigation by the RS MUP -- well, let me strike that. You know there was no investigation by the RS MUP, official investigation, into Srebrenica events in July, August, September, October, November, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't, not an official one. We could not do that. There was no possibility because of the war, and we did not have the powers, but regardless of the powers or authority, I started this in 1995. And you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. You answered. There wasn't any. I want to show you one. Could I have P06426. I'm not going to spend a lot of time on this, but this is an interview with you. David Rhode was prosecuted in Republika Srpska, investigated by state security, Goran Radovic, who you know, and others, arrested, charged and eventually pardoned by the president. And in this press conference in November, you were asked about David Rhode, and I'll let you read it. I'm not going to read it all out, but you said: "David Rhode has been arrested primarily due to false -- primarily due to false documents and unauthorised entry into Republika Srpska. And, please, that does not mean we are against journalists visiting our territories, but we are against the spies having journalists' passage." I'll skip a sentence: "Your colleague was performing the most difficult form of espionage for which the sentence from 3 to 15 years of prison is foreseen in Republika Srpska in peacetime. So consider it yourselves." I'll skip a sentence: "We will not and we cannot accept people who are working outside of their journalist etiquette and openly against my people and this state." And then you said David Rhode was lucky. So this is when you're minister of the interior, this is when you know about the mass executions, and your MUP, the only Prosecution it's done for Srebrenica, is of a journalist who took photos of the Pilica dam execution site and tried to find out what had happened; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in the way it's formulated in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he takes pictures -- and I'm not going to go through the whole court file. Some of it is in evidence. He takes pictures of the dam and of the area around Orahovac and he's arrested. And for trying to show where execution sites are, you say he openly -- working openly against your people and the state.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The services -- I cannot remember much about this event and I'm not sure that journalists or newspapers, especially "Oslobodjenje" reported in an adequate manner my views. For me, at the time, this was just a short information and an unimportant event. So that the only thing that this could have happened was the legal action against him, against this journalist, so I did not get especially involved in this. It was a matter for the State Security Service. I didn't issue an order for his arrest or his release or anything. It just followed its normal course. So I cannot say anything particular about this, that I was involved in such cases in that period. This was the legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I misspoke, I'm sorry, at line 20 page 86, I said "Pilica dam," I meant "Petkovci dam." Nothing further at the moment. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I ask Mr. Karadzic to re-examine you, I have a couple of questions. Shall we show him the 2010 interview, page 43, 25350. There may be no point because it's in English. It's a conversation why you did not tell Mr. Karadzic about the protest or the -- about the Beara's request to use some MUP forces for illegal activities including liquidation, et cetera, and so why you didn't tell Mr. Karadzic when you met him on 13th, 14th, 15th. Do you remember having discussed that? So I'll read out --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll read out the passage: "So let me get this straight, is the reason you are saying that you did not discuss or protest to the president what was happening with the army killing people because you thought he already knew from all these other sources?" Other sources you discussed Bajagic or other people, Deronjic, and this is your answer as recorded, and you confirmed that, I quote: "This is crystal clear because he had Bajagic who knew everything. He had Deronjic. He received all the information that he needed from them. Also, he had the entire nomenclature there, people who knew everything and controlled everything." So you testified today that you stood by that statement. You remember that, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. But just to make myself clear, my statement that he had those who could have informed him, not that I know that they did inform him. They could have reported to him about all events that they had information about. And the reason -- another reason why I did not believe about Beara's act was that at that moment I didn't -- because I prevented the police from getting involved, I did not have any information that he did do it. I had the information that they could have been abused. That was the reason in that short interval why I had no reported to President Karadzic about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll read out again to you what was said, the question by the investigator: "Because you thought he already knew from all these other sources?" And your answer: "This is crystal clear."

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, to make myself clear, it's completely clear that he had sources to obtain information from, and whether specifically he knew that Beara, that I believed that someone had reported to him that Beara had requested police in order to commit the execution of prisoners, not that. So it's crystal clear that he had sources of information which were supposed to inform him about everything. But I didn't -- I don't know how this was interpreted nor did I think that he did receive this specific information, that Beara shot prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. My second question is about your statement in your witness statement tendered today by Mr. Karadzic, but I will allow you to read that statement later on, if necessary, and that means you do not need to consult that statement at the moment. At certain point -- part of your statement, you referred to your meeting with Mr. Karadzic in the spring of 1996, where you discussed the -- about what happened or the crimes following the fall of Srebrenica, and Mr. Karadzic expressed his disappointment. Do you remember having said that? It's --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. That was in spring, I think in April, March or April, thereabouts. I mean, that was an unofficial conversation. I wasn't still working in the ministry, or, rather, not working but I wasn't in a position, so this was an unofficial visit to the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
