utterances.text: Could you tell us in concrete terms what you discussed with Mr. Karadzic? What did he say and what did you say? Please let us know the conversation, in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was on an informal visit. After a while, I appeared for the first time again, and in addition to a series of other questions in an informal conversation, I believe that at some point I touched on the army and Beara and their conduct. That was a brief reaction on the part of the president. He was dissatisfied. He said that they had jeopardised the state, and that was all that we exchanged, to the best of my recollection of the time. It wasn't any kind of official conversation. It was unofficial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I know it's an unofficial conversation after your dismissal. You said you touched on the army and Beara and their conduct. Could you be more specific as to what you said to Mr. Karadzic, in real -- in concrete terms? Please be as specific as possible, as far as you remember.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was concrete about their -- their attitude at that time and the previous time, their attitude to the president and his orders, and at one point I touched on -- I touched on his -- in fact, his conduct in the Srebrenica area and what he did with the prisoners of war. I could see from the conversation that the President Karadzic was already aware of that because that was the end of March or April 1996. I didn't tell him anything new at the time. I just remember his reaction that he reacted to them by saying that they were negating the state by such an attitude, and that was all the conversation we had about this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who was "he," when you said his conduct, his orders, and his conduct in the Srebrenica area, what he did with the prisoners. Who was he? Mladic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had primarily Beara in mind. He was in the focus of my attention, but, of course, in all this, in everything that was going on, certainly Mladic's responsibility was great, as the commander, that he allowed all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So by this time, you already knew the locations of execution sites because you came to know as a result of your secret operative investigation in the previous year? So I take it you must have discussed it with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my replacement, there was no need for me or wish for me to do anything any longer officially. I was just telling you about this informal conversation, and we did not discuss the execution sites. We just briefly touched on the army but we did not discuss the execution site and I realised that this process was ongoing and that the president was informed at the point. It was March or April. So I had the impression that he was aware about this process of clearing up everything about Srebrenica. But as I say, I was there only for a short while, on an informal visit, and after that, once again, I left Republika Srpska and I went to Belgrade where I had already been living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that Mr. Karadzic expressed disappointment. Why was he disappointed? For what?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this subject, the army and the command structure, is something that I touched on and he was disappointed by the entire structure. He was disappointed by the structure and by their overall conduct, their conduct, their attitude in general, and jeopardising the state. It was -- as I say, it was an informal conversation, and so this disappointment was not only formal but also something human expressed by a man who was disappointed by a group of people. He was not disappointed in the institution but it was this group of people that disappointed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was in paragraph 133 of your statement, could you take a look at it? You have your statement with you, 133. It reads like this: After a while, I discussed with President Karadzic the allegations about crimes following the fall of Srebrenica. By the time -- by that time, you already knew that there were crimes, crimes were committed, but why did you put the allegations about crimes? Why did you put allegations? Do you deny that there were crimes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't deny. Perhaps the word, the formulation, was imprecise. I don't deny, no. I did not have in mind everything that was correct, but the knowledge and the terms, "allegations," I imply everything that has already been proved through investigation, so perhaps the term was not well applied. Perhaps the word was not a good choice. Something that wasn't proved already. But only information, information about crimes, that would have been a better word, perhaps, than allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac. I take it you have some re-examination, Mr. Karadzic? By the way, but do you think you can finish your re-examination today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I would ask for a couple of follow-up questions based on Your Honour's questions on these two topics, wouldn't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before the re-examination, for the benefit of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Further cross-examination by Mr. Nicholls:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You just answered in quite detail, in quite a lot of detail, His Honour Judge Kwon's questions about para 133 of your statement, and the last sentence there is: We did not have other talks about Srebrenica, other than this one in the spring of 1996. I want to go over what you said on this very topic in your 2010 interview, 65 ter 25350, e-court page 146, and we should maybe bring that up, even though it's only in English: Question: Did you ever discuss what happened with President Karadzic? Tomo Kovac: About Srebrenica? Question: Yes. No, is the answer. Okay. Tomo Kovac: Because I was not going to fall into the trap. I had some short informal conversations with him, although the army should have come under the same way, duh, duh, duh. Same interview, same 65 ter number, pages 149 to 150. Question: Okay, you said a moment ago just before we showed you the Borovcanin promotion that you never spoke with Karadzic about Srebrenica, you didn't want to fall into that trap because it was all under military jurisdiction. Then you said, quote, "Well I had several short conversations," quote. So did you talk to Karadzic about Srebrenica or not later on? Question: Officially or unofficially is the next question to you. Answer: It was always unofficially -- unofficially and it was always about Beara. Question: Okay. When? Next page, please. Maybe in September 1995 in Banja Luka when I was talking about Beara when Beara presented a threat. I touched upon his stupidities. We had no other conversation than this about Srebrenica. And what did Karadzic say? Nothing. He just made a gesture with his hand, and as if he didn't want to listen about it. That's about it. That's what you said in 2010. You started off your testimony by saying you were truthful in your statements, in those interviews. You have just given a completely different account to the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I talked about Beara in September because I had the information that he was preparing a coup in Banja Luka, and it was about those circumstances of his conduct. And while he was security element in Montenegro, and he was preparing for a civil war to break out among the Serbs, so that was what I was telling him about briefly, judged on the operative intelligence, not that I discussed this aspect of his activities and his crimes in Srebrenica, just to make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] okay. Let's see how clear it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So when I asked you: So did you talk to Karadzic about Srebrenica or not, later on, and you said, maybe in September, September 1995 in Banja Luka, we had no other conversation than this about Srebrenica, you were talking about a civil war that Beara was trying to start? Is that serious?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what that mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I asked you if you talked about President Karadzic -- with President Karadzic about Srebrenica, you said in September 1995, you started bringing up Beara, and the president waved his hand like he didn't want to talking about it. Were you lying to me or were you not telling the truth in court right now? And both times you said you only talked about Srebrenica once.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said to you that I had discussed with Karadzic the crimes in Srebrenica. I discussed Beara. And it's not all right for you to put two questions that I'm supposed to be -- let us deal with facts and be clear. One thing is the talk about Beara; the other thing is the talk about Srebrenica. In the whole of Republika Srpska was under --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: Your answer was: Maybe -- to the question of whether you ever talked to about -- with Karadzic about Srebrenica. Your answer was: Maybe in September of 1995 in Banja Luka, and then you go on about Beara and being a threat. And you say: We had no other conversations than this about Srebrenica. That meaning is clear, isn't it? You were telling me you spoke to Karadzic once about Srebrenica and that was in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection. None of this is true. None of this is correct. The paragraph does not read like that, not in English and not in Serbian. And it was interpreted by Mr. Nicholls differently: [In English] "Maybe in 1995 in Banja Luka when I was talking about Beara, when Beara presented a threat. I touched upon his stupidities. We had no other conversations than this about Srebrenica." [Interpretation] The witness says maybe I touched upon Srebrenica when I was talking about Beara in general; whereas Mr. Nicholls says you confirm that you discussed him then. And he said instead: I may have touched upon it. We should look at the Serbian version. That would be the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you wish, you can hear the audio tape. And you can deal with it in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me ask you: When you spoke to me about when you -- when you spoke to the OTP about when you talked to President Karadzic about Srebrenica, it was maybe September 1995 when this coup was being planned, when the civil war was going to break out. That's September, not April of the next year. When you meet with the Defence and they take a statement from you, the time of this conversation is moved back to April, exactly when President Karadzic's first and only investigative request comes out. Did the Defence suggest to you this might have been April, in fact?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, and you are twisting, distorting, everything, as you did when you examined me before. You put a different stress on every word. I told you I may have touched upon Srebrenica. I didn't mean crimes in Srebrenica. I touched upon Beara's inclination to misuse and abuse, but it was not discussion about Srebrenica. It was discussion about Beara as a threat. Srebrenica was certainly not a topic. Those are two different events which cannot be linked, and the Defence could not have suggested anything to me. I am not susceptible to suggestion. I'm not that type of person. I'm not even susceptible to your suggestions, although you have been trying for ten years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 88, His Honour Judge Kwon asked you about the portion where you discussed Karadzic's sources and how things were crystal clear. And Judge Kwon asked -- said to you, His Honour Judge Kwon. I'll read out again to you what was said, the question by the investigator, because you thought he already knew from all these sources and your answer this is crystal clear. This is your answer now today in court: Once again, to make myself clear, it's completely clear that he had sources to obtain information from, and whether specifically he knew that Beara -- that I believed that someone had reported to him that Beara had requested police in order to commit the execution of prisoners, not that. So it's crystal clear that he had sources of information which were supposed to inform him about everything, but I didn't -- I don't know how this was interpreted, nor did I think that he did receive the specific information that Beara shot prisoners. Could we have page 50 of this 2010 interview. Talking about the same topic, this is your meeting with President Karadzic on the 14th, 15th: Okay, this is the question, top of the page, from investigator, Did you tell president about Beara's request during this meeting? Answer: I cannot remember whether I told him. But I just know that he was aware of my constant criticisms of Beara, but I cannot remember, but he must have known. He must have known. It was -- it must have been known what Beara's behaviour on the war front was. Each of us had at least ten lines of informing. So we all knew what was going on. I knew about Kravica, other people knew about Kravica, and there is no way he could not have known about Beara's behaviour. So you have once again, for the hundredth time today, changed your story.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's true, and even a minute ago, when you were stating what my evidence of today, you misrepresent it. You play with words. I have been saying the same thing all over and over again, and I'm telling the truth so I see no reason for you to suggest something like this. Do you have any more questions? You have been just characterising my evidence today and my evidence given before. What do you want me to do, to confirm that I'm lying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop commenting, please, and answer the question I just asked you. I will read out what you just said in this session to Judge Kwon about Beara and whether President Karadzic would have known from his sources about Beara and the executions: So it's crystal clear that he, the president, had sources of information which were supposed to inform him about everything, but I didn't -- I don't know how this was interpreted, nor did I think that he did receive this specific information, that Beara shot prisoners. And here, you're asked whether you're told about Beara's request and about his request to execute prisoners, and you say he must have known, it was -- it must have been known what Beara's behaviour on the war front was. Each of us had at least ten lines of informing, so we all knew what was going on. I knew about Kravica, other people knew about Kravica, and there was no way he could not have known about Beara's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that legally speaking he should have known, and if we later established, both you and I, that the military system was shut, closed, even up to the Main Staff level, it's clear that he didn't receive this information from them. If they had worked in accordance with the law, he should have received it; but since they were not acting in accordance with the law, since they had isolated the whole system, he did not receive it or may have not received it. Mr. Karadzic himself can tell us whether he got that report from them or not. I was just saying in my evidence that if things had been done lawfully, he should have had that information, whereas you are misstating my evidence, quoting me, or, rather, misquoting me as saying that he had received it. I could not confirm that years ago and I cannot confirm today the things that I don't know. And one of the things I don't know is what kind of information he received. I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last question. One, I'm not misquoting you or mis-citing. I'm reading back what you said in interviews and what you said in this courtroom. Two, what you're telling me is that when were you asked about whether you spoke about what Beara was doing and requesting help from the MUP to execute prisoners, when you say, But he must have known. He must have known, it must have known what Beara's behaviour on the war front was, each of us had ten lines of informing, so we all knew what was going on. I knew about Kravica, other people knew Kravica. There was no way he could have known about Beara's behaviour, what you were trying to say truthfully was no way he could not have known about Beara's behaviour, what you were trying to truthfully say was I don't think he could have possibly gotten that information? That's what you just kind of put to us.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formulate your sentences clearly. Give me two questions or two answers. If that is a problem, I'll tell you clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sure, okay.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are using police talk. Maybe others will not understand us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. This is pretty simple. I'll break it down further. When you gave this answer about did you tell the president about Beara's request during your meeting, and you said each of us had ten lines of informing, so we all knew what was going on, let me put it this way -- strike that. When you say about the president there was no way he could not have known about Beara's behaviour, what does that mean? What were you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say this: If the military security and the Main Staff of the VRS had acted lawfully, he should have had that information. At that moment, I was not aware of the extent of the conspiracy designed by Beara and those around him, which completely prevented this system from functioning. Later on, through my operative investigations and through this and other trials, I realised that they had completely isolated themselves within their system. They closed it off. It did not act in accordance with the law. But under the law, if they had respected it, they had to inform him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation of what you meant when you said there was no way he could not have known about Beara's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're through, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's plan. How long do you need, Mr. Karadzic, for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I doubt that I would finish it today. If I did have 35 minutes, I could have done it, but now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Lazarevic, you have to fly to Serbia today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You are right about -- well, if need be, I mean, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm thinking about extending the sitting for today, if everybody is in agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That would be very convenient if it's for like 20 minutes or something that I think that I will be able to catch my flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, shall we try to finish by 3.00, then? Mr. Karadzic said 45 minutes or 35 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you inform me of the option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I asked him if he could be here on Monday and he said he basically could, once he got the authorisation from the Tribunal. So I think instead of rushing Dr. Karadzic, it's better to just continue on Monday with the redirect examination, or if you want to use some time today, but not to force Dr. Karadzic to complete it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, do you have any problem with staying over the weekend at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that Mr. Karadzic prefers to start his re-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency, thank you. Not to be rushed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will do so. So, again, my advice is still valid not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
